newsitem.title: USA: California Senate paves way for state tobacco suits.
newsitem.headline: California Senate paves way for state tobacco suits.

text.p: California's Senate Thursday approved a bill to eliminate the special immunity from product liability lawsuits enjoyed by tobacco products in the state.

The state Senate approved the bill, by Sen. Quentin Kopp, on a vote of 28-to-9, his office said. The bill now advances to the Assembly Judiciary Committee, where it could be taken up in the coming weeks.

If passed by the Assembly and signed by Gov. Pete Wilson, Kopp's bill would remove an obstacle preventing Republican state Attorney General Dan Lungren from filing a state lawsuit against the tobacco companies, lawmakers said.

The current immunity for tobacco products was part of 1987 legislation intended to curtail the number of product liability lawsuits by granting immunity to the manufacturers of certain products. In addition to tobacco, other consumer products, including sugar, castor oil, alcohol and butter, were included in the immunity legislation.
Lungren has steadfastly maintained that the immunity provided by the 1987 state law bars California from joining other states in lawsuits against major tobacco companies.
But pressure has been building in recent months on state lawmakers to join the legal battle. Earlier this year, the state legislature passed nonbinding resolutions calling on Lungren to act.
Kopp's bill, supported by the California Medical Association and other groups, would specifically end the liability protection for tobacco products.
"The Senator is confident it will be approved by the Assembly," said Randall Henry, Kopp's legislative consultant.

There are an estimated 4 million smokers in California. According to a recent study by the University of California, state taxpayers spent $4.1 billion in Medi-Cal expenses between 1980 and 1993 to treat smoking-related illnesses.
